statement: What is the largest number of different whole numbers that can be chosen from 1 to 20 so that no chosen number is exactly twice another chosen number?

choices.misconception: I chose 11 to 20 and assumed nothing smaller could be added.
I took the ten odd numbers and then added only 4 and 16, missing 12 and 20.
I chose 11 to 20 and then added 3, 4 and 5, but missed that 1 can be added too.
I removed only one number from each chain like 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, but the longest chain needs two removed.

hints: Group the numbers into doubling chains like 3, 6, 12.

Every number is an odd number times a power of 2, so the numbers split into chains where each is double the one before. Choices in different chains never clash, so maximise inside each chain separately.
The chains are 1-2-4-8-16, 3-6-12, 5-10-20, 7-14, 9-18 and the single numbers 11, 13, 15, 17, 19. In a chain you can take every other number.

solutions.reliable: Write each number as an odd number times a power of 2. The chains are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 (take 1, 4, 16: three), 3, 6, 12 (two), 5, 10, 20 (two), 7, 14 (one), 9, 18 (one), and 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 (one each, five). Numbers in different chains are never double each other, so the maximum is 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 14. The transferable idea: split the set into independent pieces, find the best in each, and add.
solutions.elegant: Take 11 to 20, which works, then add every number from 1 to 10 whose double is 10 or less and whose half is not chosen: 1, 3, 4 and 5. That gives 14, and the chains show nothing better exists.

whyOnTest: Extremal selection problems test whether you find the structure, here doubling chains, that makes the maximum provable rather than guessed.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
